name: Sam Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don’t sell anything or campaign for a side. What you share is confidential; I’d like your public view and your private thoughts.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Sam Weber, twenty-seven, a carpentry crew lead with a trade certificate. I share a rented house with my partner Jo; there are no children. I’ve built a savings reserve and earn well for this work, though I know not everyone on site has that buffer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Describe a normal day at work. What do you enjoy and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I check the drawings, walk the work area, and make sure the crew has the right materials before we start. I like watching a new carpenter gain confidence with a tricky stair stringer. I get worn down by last-minute schedule changes that leave the crew waiting without pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say I’m fine with an AI tool that checks a materials count, as long as a worker checks what is delivered. A short form is useful if it gives the crew more time to do the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don’t expect a few routine tasks to change my hours. I have a strong reserve and there are many builders nearby, but I still want workers to benefit if a contractor saves time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the crew and test the count checker on our next supply order. I’d bring the result to the shop steward if it saved time, so we could ask whether the saved hours return to workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about a small tool changing the paperwork. My bigger concern is whether the crew gets a fair share of any time it saves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare the count against?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d compare it with the signed order and the delivery ticket. If a pack is missing, I’d write it down before anyone signs that everything arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a faster process if the saved time went only to the contractor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the steward to raise it, because efficiency should not mean workers lose paid hours. I can understand a company wanting to save money. The people doing the work should share in the benefit.

say: I’d use a checker if a worker still checks the **delivery**.
I want the crew to gain time for the **job itself**.
think: I don’t expect these routine tasks to change **my hours**.
I want workers to share any **time savings**.
do: Keep leading the crew and test the **AI count checker** on the next order.
Ask the **shop steward** about saved time if the tool helps.
feel: I feel **calm** about the paperwork change, with fairness on my mind.
S0.quote: The people doing the work should share in the benefit.
fieldNote: Sam links a small efficiency gain to **worker benefit**.
His reserve makes a routine change manageable, though he notices that not every worker has **the same buffer**.

steps.text: Keep leading the carpentry crew on active work
Test the AI count checker on the next supply order
Ask the shop steward to raise how saved hours benefit workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say contractors should talk with workers before they change schedules or buying systems. I want the union involved in setting clear rules for training and checking safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do planning and records as lead, so some desk tasks may shrink. I’m paid well and have savings, but the crew could still lose hours if the contractor changes how many leads it needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the union steward to meet the contractor about paid training and safety checks. I’d learn the schedule system if it helps me coordinate the crew, and I’d keep an eye on actual hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about records and scheduling changing, but I have some control through training and the union. I’d be more concerned about workers with little savings if hours fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want included in a training agreement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want training on paid time, a worker able to challenge a bad schedule, and no silent cut to hours while people learn. The agreement should cover apprentices as well as people who lead crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the card say AI will make fewer construction sites open?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn’t state that. I’d track actual work and ask the contractor before blaming the technology for a change in starts.

say: I’d want workers involved before contractors change **schedules**.
I want the union to set rules for **training and safety**.
think: I do **planning and records**, so some of my tasks may shrink.
I worry about crew hours even with **my savings**.
do: Ask the union steward to meet the contractor about **paid training**.
Learn the **schedule system** if it helps the crew.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, with some control through training and union input.
S1.quote: The agreement should cover apprentices as well as people who lead crews.
fieldNote: Sam’s central concern is **shared rules** for workers at different levels.
He does not infer fewer starts and wants changes tied to **actual hours**, with written agreements for workers.

steps.text: Ask the union to negotiate paid training and safety checks
Learn the schedule system used to coordinate the crew
Keep leading carpentry work while the contractor has projects

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say workers need a voice in what happens to jobs and hours. I’d ask the union to negotiate paid notice and support rather than promise that any trade is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI could take planning and records in my lead role by 2028. Robots arrive around 2031, so the carpentry work is exposed too, and my income is not guaranteed just because I have experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask the union to seek notice and a fair transition plan. In 2029 I’d check my hours and contact other builders if the contractor had cut the crew’s work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about both dates, though my savings give me more room than some of my crew have. I’d use the time to seek a fair plan rather than act as if my experience guarantees work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could another builder be a lasting safe job if robots arrive in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d treat a new opening as paid work for now, not protection from the later date. I’d use the reserve to avoid rushing into a bad offer, while still applying if someone is hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Jo change if your income fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d pause replacing our old bathroom fixtures and keep the housing costs covered. I’d rather spend from savings for a short gap than borrow to keep a renovation moving.

say: I’d want workers to have a **voice in job changes**.
I’d ask the union to negotiate **notice and support**.
think: I expect AGI to take planning and records from **my lead role** in 2028.
I know carpentry is exposed when **robots arrive**.
do: Ask the union to seek **notice** and a fair transition plan.
Keep crew work and contact **other builders** if hours fall in 2029.
Pause **bathroom fixture purchases** if household income falls.
feel: I feel **anxious about both dates**, though my reserve gives me room.
S2.quote: I’d use the reserve to avoid rushing into a bad offer, while still applying if someone is hiring.
fieldNote: Sam recognizes that experience does not guarantee **future work**.
His savings and union provide options but neither can guarantee **continued work** or a safe new job.

steps.text: Ask the union to negotiate notice and a transition plan
Keep leading the crew while work remains
Contact other builders if crew hours are cut in 2029
Pause the bathroom fixture replacement if income falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives workers and contractors time to agree on training and notice. I want the apprentice to hear what is changing from the people responsible for the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI reaches the records and planning in 2031, with robots reaching carpentry around 2034. The longer warning helps me build my reserve, but I can’t treat either the desk work or the craft as permanently safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the crew and take paid training when the contractor explains the new system. In 2032 I’d review my hours and talk with the union if the roster had changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about the eventual robot date, but five years gives me time to act with the crew. My savings help, and I don’t want them to make me complacent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years before robots change for your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d have more time to keep earning and to add to savings. Jo and I could delay the bathroom work rather than borrow, but that depends on our actual pay and costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move into planning as a safe fallback after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn’t call planning safe when AGI does thinking work. I’d learn systems for my current role and use union advice to understand which real jobs are open.

say: I’d want a **training and notice agreement** before hours change.
I want apprentices to hear directly from **site leaders**.
think: I expect AGI to reach records and planning in **2031**.
I can’t call either desk work or craft **permanently safe**.
do: Keep leading the crew and take **paid training** on the new system.
Talk with the **union** if the roster changes.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though five years gives time to act together.
S3.quote: I’d learn systems for my current role and use union advice to understand which real jobs are open.
fieldNote: Sam uses extra time for **collective preparation** and wants the training to support apprentices as well as leads.
He sees desk planning as exposed and asks the union for **current job information**.

steps.text: Keep leading the crew while contracts continue
Complete paid training on the contractor’s new system
Ask the union about roster changes and open jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years gives the union and contractors time to plan paid training and fair notice. I’d keep learning tools that help the crew today without telling apprentices that any path is guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can build a larger reserve in ten years, but AGI still takes planning in 2036 and robots reach carpentry around 2039. I don’t know which jobs will remain, so I won’t assume a desk role protects me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep working, save more, and stay involved in the union’s training talks. In 2037 I’d review the local job list and contact other builders if my hours were reduced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives me a useful runway, but I’m still uneasy about what happens after 2039. I’d keep my savings and make decisions when I know what the contractor is actually offering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Jo decide before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d decide whether to renovate the bathroom or keep that money in savings. We have no children or fixed wedding plan, so we can decide based on our work and the cost at the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a long course during the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take training if it has a clear job use and decent pay. I wouldn’t empty our reserve for an office course when full AGI changes thinking work.

say: I’d use the decade to plan **training and notice** with the union.
I wouldn’t tell apprentices that any **career is guaranteed**.
think: I can grow my reserve before **2036**.
I don’t assume an office role protects me after **full AGI**.
do: Review local jobs in 2037 and contact builders if **hours fall**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the later date, with time to plan.
S4.quote: I’d keep learning tools that help the crew today without telling apprentices that any path is guaranteed.
fieldNote: Sam sees a decade for **planning and bargaining**, not certainty, and wants workers involved in transition terms.
He and Jo can delay home improvements rather than draw down **all savings**.

steps.text: Keep leading the crew while contracts continue
Add to savings from current wages
Stay involved in union training discussions
Contact other builders if my hours are reduced in 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because two years gives little time before the thinking work changes and robots follow. Paid training, clear notice and a worker voice in staffing decisions would help the crew plan without relying on each person’s savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I’d ask how we protect apprentices as well as experienced workers. A fair transition should include people who are still learning the trade, not only the people who already have a title.

headlineQuote: A fair transition should include people who are still learning the trade, not only the people who already have a title.
portrait: Sam is a **27-year-old** crew lead with high pay and a strong carpentry reputation.
He lives with Jo and has a **strong reserve**.
He supports union bargaining and **worker voice** while using proven tools selectively.
His reserve helps, but the robot timeline still threatens **hands-on carpentry**.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture worries Sam most because it leaves little time before thinking work changes.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **training and notice** would help Sam’s crew plan for change.
